title: The Eight-Second Tour
protagonist: The sports director of Greg LeMond's team (a role; no named person, no invented quotes)
primary_metric: predicted average speed (km/h) over the 24.5 km under the scenario model, read against the break-even speed the 50-second target requires

options.A: Aero Bars -- commit LeMond to the aero-bar position: lower drag, less sustainable power
options.B: Full Power -- ride the conventional position at full power

reinforcement_note: At write time (2026-10-03) a live query of readmodel/standards_spine.json found zero skills at n==0 anywhere in the 322-skill spine, so new_coverage[] is honestly empty rather than padded. Adjacent thin skills were checked against this case's real deliverables: Exponent (also Power) n=8 and How to evaluate an exponential expression n=8 are forced by D2/D5 (the cube law); How to solve a multi-step equation with a variable on one side n=4 by D3; How to identify the slope of a line n=6 and How to write a linear equation given a set of data n=10 by D4 (the cube-law break-even points are exactly collinear, slope = the D2 power factor). Other thin skills in the same groups (system of equations, how to solve a system of linear equations, scientific notation) were reviewed and are NOT forced by any deliverable, so they are not claimed.

sources.claim: Aerodynamic losses outweigh power losses at cycling speeds above 46 km/h; below 30 km/h a more upright time-trial position is beneficial (models from 19 TT cyclists, torso angles 0-24 degrees)

sources.note: Abstract read via NCBI efetch (PMID 24726654, J Biomech 47(8):1894-8). The abstract contains the 46 km/h crossover and NO 14% power figure; the 'peak power fell about 14%' claim from the concept sheet was NOT verifiable and is not used. Does not compare aero bars with a conventional position.

not_found: A peer-reviewed measurement of sustainable-power loss for aero bars versus a conventional position -- none found; became MA3 (range 3-14%, lower bound the author's own).

Fintelman et al. 2014 'peak power fell about 14% between 24 degrees and a flat torso' -- concept-sheet claim not present in the abstract on PubMed; not used. The 14% upper end of y is the author's assumption.
A source for the bundle model parameters (CdA 0.32, Crr 0.004, mass 78 kg) -- scenario values from the internal sports bundle; stated as MA4, not cited.
Fignon's expected time as a director would have known it -- unknowable; hindsight stand-in disclosed (MA1).

A source for what equipment LeMond/Fignon used in the prologue and stage 15 ITTs -- not stated on the Wikipedia pages; the case says so and does not treat any earlier ITT as a pure conventional-position ride.
excluded_sources: Popular '15-25%' aero-bar CdA-reduction figures: not peer reviewed; mentioned only as not used.
ProCyclingStats stage results: not openly licensed; Wikipedia used instead.
Any 'about a minute' claim for the gain from aero bars: unsourced and cut. The case never states how many seconds the bars gained LeMond.
Fignon's saddle sores, ponytail and sleep: contested context, kept out of the math (ponytail not used).
scenario_constructions: Hindsight scenario: the real 27:55 stands in for the rival's expected stage 21 time; LeMond's conventional-position speed is Fignon's times a baseline ratio b from the three earlier 1989 ITTs (MA1, revised after Tier 2 P2). The director is a role; the case invents no quotes.
The model's absolute watts (about 728 W at 26:57) do not describe LeMond; the case uses ratios only.
The twist (a lab estimate of 12.5% drag cut and 14% power loss) is an invented hypothetical, labeled as such to the room; it is not a fact about 1989.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Hindsight stand-in and baseline: the rival's expected stage 21 time is Fignon's real 27:55, and LeMond's conventional-position speed is Fignon's speed times a baseline ratio b taken from the three earlier 1989 ITTs
modeling_assumptions.basis: REVISED 2026-10-03 (P2 fix): the earlier MA1 assumed exactly equal conventional speeds, leaving Full Power with no route to the 50 s bar by construction. A director could not have known Fignon's stage 21 time but could know the earlier ITT record. Caveats: distance, terrain, form and (stage 5) equipment differ, so b is an indicative range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The 50 s test is sensitive to this value; the A-versus-B speed comparison is not (b cancels).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Fractional cut in drag area (x) from the aero position
modeling_assumptions.basis: A peer-reviewed 14% drag change (S3) was measured for position changes among time-trial positions, not aero bars vs conventional; it anchors the range, it is not a measurement.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Fractional loss in sustainable power (y) in the aero position
modeling_assumptions.basis: No source found that measures this for aero bars vs conventional. The 3% lower bound is the case author's own assumption; the 14% upper end is also an assumption (a secondhand 14% power figure could not be confirmed in the Fintelman abstract).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The answer is sensitive to this value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Power-model parameters: air density 1.225, CdA 0.32, Crr 0.004, mass 78 kg
modeling_assumptions.basis: Typical scenario values for a rider and bike on flat ground; not LeMond's. They do not reproduce his real speed.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Break-even tolerances depend on the rolling-resistance share these parameters set.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Flat course, no wind, steady speed, no drafting
modeling_assumptions.basis: Simplification for tractable arithmetic. Wikipedia describes the weather on stage 21 as hot, dry and still (S6).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The real course and weather are ignored.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Only handlebar position changes; helmet and wheels held equal
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Real equipment differences (Appendix A) are ignored.

sensitivity_note: No SPEC Section 6 subject-matter sensitivity applies. Care point: real riders; stay on the sourced record and treat Fignon's condition as contested.

balance.argument_a: At 54.5 km/h the literature leans aero (Fintelman: aero losses outweigh power losses above 46 km/h) and the cube law makes each point of drag cut worth about 1.1 points of power. Averaged over the Appendix D box the aero position is about 1.5% faster, and it is faster than conventional in about 85% of the box; at the midpoints (x 12.5%, y 8.5%) A is predicted 1.50% faster. Only A can reach the 50 s bar at all: the conventional baseline alone gains at most about 18 s on Fignon (b 1.0109), 32 s short.
balance.argument_b: Full Power is the known quantity: the aero position's power loss is unmeasured (MA3) and untested for this rider tonight, and the aero position is slower than conventional wherever y exceeds roughly x (about 15% of the box; worst case about 26 s slower, at x 10%, y 14%). A decision rule that protects the downside (best worst case) picks B; one that maximizes expected or minimax regret (A's worst regret 26 s vs B's worst regret 72 s) picks A. Neither cited study compares aero bars with a conventional position. Honest weakness: even at the best observed baseline B gains only about 18 s of the 50 needed, so B cannot reach the bar and its case is risk and evidence, not reaching the target.
balance.margin_basis: Predicted speed from the cube-law model: B = Fignon's speed (24.5 km in 27:55) times the baseline b (midpoint of the observed range, 1.00545); A = B x ((1-y)/(1-x))^(1/3) with x=12.5%, y=8.5%. margin = 100 x (A-B)/B. b cancels in the margin.
balance.twist_effect: Twist: a team physiologist's lab estimate (hypothetical, invented for the exercise) supplies BOTH dials: drag-area cut 12.5% and power loss 14%, both inside the Appendix D ranges. A's speed falls to 52.64 km/h vs B's 52.94 (ratio about 0.994): the winner flips to B by 0.58%. The twist supplies x and y together so no reading of the case's assumptions leaves the verdict unchanged (a bare 'power loss 14%' would not flip the verdict for a drag cut of 14-15%). Facilitator only; never in case.md.
balance.stability: Base margin (1.50%) is a direct function of x and y via sensitivity_model.py; the baseline b cancels. Halving x (6.25%) and raising y by half (12.75%) each flip the winner; the other two flexes widen A's lead (4.04%, 3.05%). No flex breaches the 20% cap. The verdict is unstable and the case says so.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA2: the true drag-area cut for the aero position cannot be known before the ride and no source measures aero bars against a conventional position. Flexing -50% (6.25%) flips the winner to B (0.81%, within cap); +50% (18.75%) widens A's lead to 4.04%, within cap. One of the two load-bearing assumptions.

MA3: the true sustainable-power loss in the aero position is an unmeasured quantity and no research can settle it before the decision. Flexing +50% (12.75%) flips the winner to B (0.10%, within cap); -50% (4.25%) widens A's lead to 3.05%, within cap. The other load-bearing assumption.

deliverables.text: A times-and-speeds table for the prologue, stage 5, stage 15 and stage 21: times in seconds (adding listed gaps), average speeds, LeMond/Fignon speed ratio per time trial, the baseline range for b from the three earlier ones, the finish time LeMond needs on stage 21, and the total speed ratio needed over Fignon's 27:55 pace.
The ratio the aero position must supply (total needed ratio divided by b at each end of the baseline range) and, using the cube law, the needed power factor stated as a percent increase for each.

A break-even table: largest power loss y for drag-area cuts of 10, 14, 15 and 20 percent under the aero-only form at both ends of the baseline range, repeated with the full two-term model for 10 and 15 percent at the lower baseline, with a comparison of the two models.

An original break-even chart (two baseline lines, the sensitivity range shaded, the student's chosen point), the equation of the lower-baseline line, its slope and meaning, the share of the range on the winning side of each line, and the decision rule used.

Model limits: the power the full model implies for LeMond's real 26:57 average speed, a judgment on whether it is sustainable (the student finds and cites a reference), and a short reflection on ratios-only, the literature's limits, and two things the model leaves out.

context_glossary.desc: The person who runs a pro cycling team from the follow car, choosing tactics and equipment. In French, a directeur sportif.
A race where each rider starts alone and is timed against the clock, with no drafting off other riders.
Narrow handlebar extensions that let a rider tuck forward with elbows in, cutting air drag at the cost of a less powerful posture.
How much air resistance a rider-and-bike presents, as drag coefficient times frontal area; a smaller drag area means less wind to push through.
The small force from tyres deforming on the road; unlike air drag, it grows only in proportion to speed.
A facility that blows controlled air past a rider or bike to measure drag.

concepts: Linear equation and slope from data
catalog.ask: LeMond trails by fifty seconds going into one last ride against the clock. Sit low on the aero bars and cut the wind, or stay up and keep your full power? The answer turns on how much power the new position costs, which nobody has measured.
